Renewables · South Africa

Land baselines for renewable sites and their grid connection lines

For independent power producers, their environmental practitioners and their lenders, a dated picture of the land on each candidate site and along the grid connection route, what was there before and roughly when, the structures a connection line would cross, and then dated progress once construction starts. A person reviews every result.

Send us your site and connection route Route and servitude baselines

The problem, in your words

The land question arrives before the first panel

“What was on this land before we optioned it?”

Clearing, cultivation, informal structures and earlier works all matter to the environmental assessment and the lender’s review. The imagery archive shows roughly when each happened.

“Our connection line crosses a dozen farms.”

A grid connection needs a route and a servitude across land that may be farmed, settled or already crossed by other services. Comparing options by what they cross saves negotiation later.

“The lender wants a land baseline.”

Projects financed by Equator Principles banks and DFIs apply the IFC Performance Standards on top of national law, and ask for a dated record of the land and any structures affected.

“We need to see progress between site visits.”

Earthworks, laydown areas and access roads change weekly during construction. Dated drone surveys compared side by side show what changed, where and when.

The South African picture

New generation needs new lines, and new servitudes

The three announcements for Bid Window 7 of the Renewable Energy Independent Power Producer Procurement Programme named preferred bidders for 1,760 MW on 23 December 2024, 1,290 MW on 21 July 2025 and 890 MW on 15 December 2025, 3,940 MW in all (DBSA, 15 December 2025). Each project needs a grid connection, and a connection line needs a route, a servitude and, often, a wayleave across another party’s servitude. Projects that sell power privately raise the same land questions.

The grid itself is expanding: the national Transmission Development Plan plans about 14,494 km of new lines, and the first Independent Transmission Projects prequalified seven bidders in December 2025. Lines that comply with the power-line standard (GN 2313) inside the strategic transmission corridors are excluded from environmental authorisation, so the land baseline for them has to come from somewhere else.

Where projects are procured

The IPP Office publishes the procurement programmes and their documents at ipp-projects.co.za. Environmental authorisation for generation facilities runs under NEMA and the EIA Regulations 2014, as amended, with a registered environmental assessment practitioner.

Site selection and due diligence

A dated land history for each candidate site

For each candidate site we assemble the documented history of the land from archived satellite imagery and open datasets: what was built, cleared or cultivated, and roughly when. A land-use and land-cover baseline maps built-up land, cropland, bare ground, water and tree cover across the site and a buffer around it, combined with the structure register.

Candidate sites and connection routes are compared side by side, by the structures they affect and by the terrain: steep and erosion-prone ground and drainage crossings from elevation data, and historically flooded or low-lying land from past satellite records. It is screening that informs the choice; the geotechnical and hydrological studies stay with your engineers.

What you receive

  • An imagery history of each site, with the dates of the scenes used
  • A land-use and land-cover baseline map
  • A comparison table of sites and connection routes
  • Slope, drainage and flood screening layers
  • A PDF report and GIS layers

Grid connection lines

What the connection route would cross

Along each connection route option, we list the structures within the servitude width and a wider band, rate each 500 m stretch for encroachment density, and map tracks, cleared ground and other services’ corridors the line would cross. Once the route is fixed, a dated register of the structures on it supports landowner engagement and, where structures are affected and lenders apply IFC Performance Standard 5, the cut-off-date records. The servitude diagram itself is a professional land surveyor’s work.

Route and servitude baselines for new lines

Construction and earthworks

Dated progress between site visits

Earthworks and progress

Dated drone orthophotos and elevation models compared side by side, with maps of where ground has been cut or filled between visits. Not a certified survey or a quantity surveyor’s valuation.

Plant and equipment

Heavy equipment visible at laydown yards and work fronts, recorded on each survey date: a snapshot of activity on the land, never tracking.

Volumes

Stockpile, spoil and borrow-pit volumes from drone elevation models, to support your surveyors. Not a statutory survey.

Drone surveys are subject to the permits and authorisations each job requires. In South Africa that means an operator with a UASOC and an Air Service Licence, the landowner’s permission for every flight, and approvals for flights within 50 m of structures, people or roads (drone law).

Fire near the site

Fire-hotspot notices and burnt-area maps

CSIR’s AFIS already gives South Africa free satellite fire information. For the sites and connection lines you name, we add notices of satellite-detected hotspots from NASA FIRMS filtered to the buffers around them, checked by a reviewer, and maps of the burnt area afterwards. It is not an emergency or early-warning service, and small, short-lived or cloud-covered fires can be missed.

Honest scope

What we do, and what we don’t

What we do

  • Document what was on the land, and roughly when
  • Compare sites and connection routes by the structures and terrain they involve
  • Record structures on the chosen route before servitude negotiations
  • Show dated construction progress between visits

What we don’t do

  • Inspect panels, turbines or electrical plant
  • Replace topographic, cadastral or geotechnical surveys
  • Verify title or tenure, or value land
  • Promise capture dates or turnaround ahead of scoping

Frequently asked questions

Is this a topographic or cadastral survey?

No. Our registers and screening layers support your engineers and your land surveyor; they do not replace a topographic survey for design or the cadastral survey behind a servitude diagram.

How far back can you show a site's history?

As far as dated archive imagery goes for that place, which varies. We report what was built, cleared or changed on the site and roughly when, from the scenes that exist, and tell you what the archive holds before you commit.

Can you work to a bid-window deadline?

We agree the schedule in the proposal and tell you at the start what the imagery for your sites allows. We do not promise turnaround before scoping, because archive coverage, cloud and, for drone work, permits set the pace.

Do you inspect panels or turbines?

No. We work on the land, mapping structures, cleared ground, earthworks, tracks and equipment visible on each survey date. Plant inspection is outside our scope.

Can the baseline go to our lenders?

Yes, as a dated, credited record that supports your environmental and social baseline and, where IFC Performance Standard 5 applies, the cut-off-date records. It does not replace the independent environmental and social consultant’s review.

Send us your site boundary and connection route

Site polygons and the connection route (Shapefile, GeoPackage, KML or GeoJSON), the options you are comparing and the date the record must reflect. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
